_about: All teaching text for the mechanism viewer and the Reactions window. Placeholders: {Nu} nucleophile, {Base} base, {LG} leaving group as drawn, {LGion} what leaves, {X} acid counter-ion, {class} substrate class (1°, 2°…), {cation}/{cation2} carbocation class before/after a shift, {via} how the chosen product formed, {product} product name, {stereo} stereo sentence, {rank} major/minor. [[term]] marks a glossary term (tap for its definition). Reviewed against standard intro textbooks after Session 3 (plan, Answers from Peter, 6).
speaker: LAB

sn2_meet.text: Meet the players. {Nu} is the [[nucleophile]]: it is rich in electrons (red cloud). The C–{LG} bond is polar, so the carbon is [[electrophile|electron-poor]] (δ+) and {LG} is δ−.
why: {LG} is more [[electronegativity|electronegative]] than carbon, so it pulls the shared electrons of the C–{LG} bond towards itself. That leaves the carbon slightly positive (δ+).
Opposite charges attract: the electron-rich {Nu} is drawn to the δ+ carbon. That pull is the dashed line.

sn2_attack.text: {Nu} attacks the δ+ carbon from the side directly opposite {LG}: a [[backside attack]]. Curved arrows show the electrons moving.
why: The empty orbital that accepts the new electrons (the C–{LG} [[antibonding orbital]], σ*) points out of the back of the carbon, away from {LG}. So the only way in is from behind.
{LG} also blocks the front side, so {Nu} can't come in there. Bulky groups on the carbon block the back too, which is why SN2 is fast for methyl and 1°, slower for {class}, and does not happen at 3°.

sn2_ts.text: The [[transition state]]: {Nu} is half-bonded and {LG} is half-gone, at the same time. This is the top of the energy hill. Only one step, so one hump: the rate depends on both {Nu} and the substrate ([[bimolecular]]).
why: Five groups crowd around one carbon here, so this arrangement is unstable: that is why it sits at the top of the hill and can't be isolated.
Because bond-making and bond-breaking happen in one step, the reaction goes faster with more {Nu} AND with more substrate. The 2 in SN2 means two species in the slow step.

sn2_product.text: {LG} leaves with the bonding electrons as {LGion}, a stable [[leaving group]]. The new C–{NuAtom} bond is made. The other three groups flipped over like an umbrella in the wind: [[Walden inversion|inversion]].
why: {LGion} is a good leaving group because it is a weak base: it is happy carrying the bonding electrons away.

{Nu} came in from the back, so it ends up on the opposite side from where {LG} was. The three other groups get pushed through to the other side. Watch it in 3D later: the 2D drawing keeps the atoms still.

sn2_result.text: Product: {product}. {stereo} SN2 is [[stereospecific]]: one starting stereoisomer gives one product stereoisomer.
why: Because every molecule is attacked from the back, every molecule inverts. No mixture is made, so the reaction is stereospecific.
R/S letters come from priority rules, so inversion does not always swap R and S. The app lets OpenChemLib work out the letters from the 3D arrangement, never by swapping them by hand.

sn2_meet_act.text: Step 2: the OH is now {LG}, a good [[leaving group]]. {Nu} is the [[nucleophile]] (red cloud). The C–O bond is very polar, so the carbon is [[electrophile|electron-poor]] (δ+).
why: OH⁻ is a strong base, so it is a poor leaving group. After activation the group that leaves is {LGion}, a weak base, so the C–O bond can break.

cat_meet.text: SN1 and E1 start the same way: no attack yet. The C–{LG} bond is polar: the carbon is δ+ and {LG} is δ−. A {class} carbon can hold a + charge well enough to let {LG} leave on its own.
why: Backside attack is blocked (3°) or too slow with a weak nucleophile, so the molecule waits until {LG} leaves by itself.
A polar [[protic solvent]] helps: its O–H groups surround and stabilise both ions as they separate.

cat_meet_act.text: Step 2: the OH is now {LG}, a good [[leaving group]]. The carbon is {class}, so it can hold a + charge: the leaving group goes first and a [[carbocation]] forms.
why: OH⁻ is a strong base, so it is a poor leaving group. Water (H₂O) is a weak base, so it leaves easily.

cat_ionise.text: {LG} leaves, taking both bonding electrons (one curved arrow, from the bond to {LG}). This is the slow step.
why: Breaking a bond into two ions costs a lot of energy, so this is the highest hump: the [[rate-determining step]].
Only the substrate is in this slow step, so the rate doesn't depend on the nucleophile or base: [[unimolecular]] (the 1 in SN1 and E1).

cat_ts1.text: [[transition state|Transition state]] 1: the C–{LG} bond is half broken. The carbon is becoming positive and {LG} is becoming {LGion}.
why: The better the carbon can hold a + charge, the lower this hump. That is why 3° > 2°, and 1°/methyl cations essentially don't form (unless allylic or benzylic).

cat_cation.text: A {cation} [[carbocation]]: the carbon has only six electrons and an empty p orbital (the two open lobes). It is flat (sp², 120°), so it can be attacked from either face.
why: The neighbouring C–H and C–C bonds feed a little electron density into the empty p orbital: [[hyperconjugation]]. More carbons on C⁺ means more of this, so 3° > 2° > 1°.
This dip in the energy hill is a real [[intermediate]], not a transition state: it lives long enough to rearrange or be trapped.

allyl_resonance.text: This cation is allylic: the + is shared between both ends of the old C=C. Two [[resonance]] forms, one real ion. A nucleophile can bond at either end, so two products form.
why: The C=C's π electrons can slide over to the C⁺. That moves the + to the far carbon. Neither drawing is the real ion: it is a blend of both.
Spreading the charge over two carbons stabilises the cation, which is why allylic (and benzylic) cations form easily.
Which end reacts more is not decided here: the app shows both products and does not rank them by end.

shift_h.text: A [[1,2-shift|hydride shift]]: an H on the next carbon moves over with its two bonding electrons (the arrow starts at the C–H bond).
why: The H moves as H⁻ (a hydride: H plus two electrons), so the carbon it leaves becomes the new C⁺.

It only happens because the new cation is more stable ({cation} → {cation2}). The app ranks products by cation stability, so the shifted product is listed as major; your answer key may list all products without ranking.

shift_alkyl.text: A [[1,2-shift|methyl (alkyl) shift]]: the group on the next carbon moves over with its two bonding electrons (the arrow starts at that C–C bond).
why: The group moves together with its bonding pair, so the carbon it leaves becomes the new C⁺.
It only happens because the new cation is more stable ({cation} → {cation2}). Only one shift per pathway is shown; several in a row are not covered yet.

shift_ring.text: A [[ring expansion]]: a ring C–C bond next to C⁺ moves over to the C⁺ (the arrow starts at that ring bond). The ring grows by one carbon.
why: The ring bond moves with its two electrons. The ring carbon it left becomes the new C⁺, now inside a bigger ring.
Two things improve: the new cation is {cation2} instead of {cation}, and a 5-membered (or smaller) ring becomes a less strained bigger ring ([[ring strain]]).
In the drawing the atoms stay put, so the new bond looks long. In the real molecule the ring relaxes into a normal six-membered shape.

shift_h_done.text: Done: the H now sits on the first carbon, and the + has moved next door. New cation: {cation2}, more stable than the {cation} one (the meter rose).
why: A shift is fast: much faster than the first step. That is why the cation can rearrange before the nucleophile or base finds it.

shift_alkyl_done.text: Done: the group has swung across, and the + has moved next door. New cation: {cation2}, more stable than the {cation} one (the meter rose).
why: A shift is fast: much faster than the first step. That is why the cation can rearrange before the nucleophile or base finds it.

shift_ring_done.text: Done: the ring is one carbon bigger and the + now sits on a ring carbon. New cation: {cation2} (the meter rose). Path: {via}.
why: Bigger, less strained ring + a more substituted cation: both help, so this is the most stable cation the app finds here.

sn1_meet_nu.text: {Nu} arrives. It is a weak [[nucleophile]], but the C⁺ is so electron-poor that even a neutral lone pair is enough.
why: The [[protic solvent]] cages anionic nucleophiles with hydrogen bonds, but here the solvent itself is the nucleophile ([[solvolysis]]).

sn1_attack.text: {Nu} donates a lone pair to the empty p orbital of C⁺. The ion is flat, so it can attack from the top or the bottom face equally.
why: Two faces, equal chance: that is why SN1 at a stereocentre gives both configurations ([[racemic]] mixture at that carbon).

sn1_ts2.text: Transition state 2: the new bond between {Nu} and the carbon is half made. This hump is lower than the first one: cations react fast.
why: Two humps with a dip between them: a two-step mechanism with an intermediate. SN2 has only one hump.

sn1_product.text: The new C–{NuAtom} bond is made, and the charge is gone. {LGion} is left in solution.
why: The product is neutral because {Nu} brought a negative charge to the positive carbon.

sn1_oxonium.text: The new C–O bond is made. The oxygen now has three bonds and a + charge (an [[oxonium ion]]). One more step: it has to lose an H⁺.
why: A neutral O with two bonds uses one lone pair to make a third bond, so it becomes positive.

sn1_deprotonate.text: [[proton transfer|Proton transfer]]: a solvent molecule pulls the extra H⁺ off the O. The product is neutral. (Worksheets often say "neglect proton transfer steps": tick the box to skip these.)
why: This is a fast acid–base step; it doesn't change the carbon skeleton or the stereo.

sn1_result.text: Product ({rank}): {product}. {stereo} SN1 is not [[stereospecific]] at the reacting carbon. Path: {via}.
why: Carbocation reactions can give several products (from shifts or resonance). The app lists each one with its own ▶ Watch button.
Major/minor comes from the cation score (more carbons on C⁺, allylic/benzylic, relieved ring strain). No percentages are claimed.

e1_base.text: A weak base ({Base}) comes close to a β-hydrogen: an H on a carbon next to C⁺. That C–H bond lines up with the empty p orbital.
why: In E1 the base doesn't need to be strong: the cation is already there, so pulling off a nearby H is easy.
Heat favours this elimination over substitution, because one molecule becomes two (more [[entropy]]).

e1_arrows.text: Two curved arrows: {Base}'s lone pair takes the H⁺, and the C–H bond's electrons swing over to make the new C=C π bond.
why: The electrons from the C–H bond fill the empty p orbital: that is the new π bond.

e1_ts2.text: Transition state 2: the C–H bond is half broken and the π bond half formed.
why: This hump is lower than the first: the slow step was losing the leaving group.

e1_product.text: The alkene is made. {Base} carries the H⁺ away (as its conjugate acid), and the charge is gone.
why: With an acid catalyst, the H⁺ given back here is the one the acid lent at the start: the acid is a [[catalyst]].
[[Zaitsev's rule]]: the more substituted alkene is more stable, so it is usually the major E1 product.
If the C=C can be E or Z, the trans (E) isomer is usually major (less crowded), but both form: the flat cation has no memory of the starting stereo.

e2_meet.text: Meet the players: {Base} is a strong [[base]]. It will not attack carbon; it will pull off a β-hydrogen (an H on a carbon next to the C–{LG} carbon). The C–{LG} bond is polar.
why: Strong, negatively charged bases (and bulky ones) favour E2. Heat helps too (two molecules become three: more [[entropy]]).

e2_anti.text: The H that leaves is drawn opposite {LG}: E2 needs the C–H and C–{LG} bonds [[anti-periplanar]] (in one plane, 180° apart).
why: Only then do the C–H bonding electrons line up with the back lobe of the C–{LG} σ* orbital, so they can flow straight into the new π bond.
In the 2D drawing the H is simply placed opposite {LG} to show the idea. Checking real 3D geometry (chairs, which H is axial, E/Z decided by geometry) is not covered yet.

e2_arrows.text: Three curved arrows, all at once: {Base} takes the H, the C–H electrons form the C=C, and {LG} leaves with its bonding pair.
why: Everything happens in one step, so there is one hump. Rate depends on both the base and the substrate ([[bimolecular]]: the 2 in E2).

e2_ts.text: The [[transition state]]: H half-transferred, π bond half-formed, C–{LG} half-broken. Top of the single hump.
why: No carbocation forms, so there are no shifts in E2.

e2_product.text: The alkene is made. {Base} now carries the H, and {LG} has left as {LGion}.
why: The leaving group must be good (a weak base) for this to be fast: I > Br > Cl, sulfonates best.
[[Zaitsev's rule]]: a small strong base gives mostly the more substituted (more stable) alkene. Other β-H's give minor products (each has its own ▶ Watch).
When the C=C can be E or Z, the app gives the trans (E-type) arrangement as major. Cases where the anti-periplanar geometry forces one isomer are not covered yet.

e2_result_hofmann.text: Product ({rank}): {product}. {stereo} Path: {via}: a bulky base takes the most reachable H, so the less substituted alkene is major ([[Hofmann product]]).
why: A bulky base like t-BuO⁻ can't reach the crowded inner H's easily, so it pulls off an H from the end CH₃.
Textbooks differ on how strongly this applies to 2° substrates; the app follows the common course rule (bulky base → Hofmann).

pro_meet.text: Step 1 (alcohol activation): OH is a poor [[leaving group]], so it can't leave as it is. The acid ({Acid}) offers an H⁺, and the O has lone pairs to grab it.
why: OH⁻ is a strong base, so it holds onto carbon. Water is a weak base, so turning OH into OH₂⁺ makes it leave easily.

pro_attack.text: [[proton transfer|Proton transfer]]: the O's lone pair takes the H⁺ from the acid; the H–{X} bond's electrons go to {X}.
why: Acid–base steps like this are very fast. Worksheets often say "neglect proton transfer steps": tick the box to skip them.

pro_done.text: The O now carries a + (OH₂⁺, an [[oxonium ion]]). The leaving group will be neutral water, a good leaving group.
why: {X}⁻ is left over. With HBr/HCl/HI it becomes the nucleophile; with H₂SO₄/H₃PO₄ the counter-ion is a very poor nucleophile, so elimination wins with heat.

pbr3_attack.text: Step 1 (alcohol activation): the O's lone pair attacks phosphorus, and one Br leaves as Br⁻.
why: P is δ+ (bonded to three electronegative Br atoms), so it's a good [[electrophile]] for the O lone pair.
One PBr₃ can activate up to three alcohol molecules; the app shows one.

pbr3_done.text: The O is now bonded to P: O(H)–PBr₂ with a + on O. That is a very good leaving group. The Br⁻ made here is the nucleophile for step 2.
why: Textbooks draw this with small differences (some remove the H⁺ first); either way the C–O bond breaks in step 2 by SN2, so the carbon is inverted. 3° alcohols are not covered (SN2 is blocked).

socl2_attack.text: Step 1 (alcohol activation): the O's lone pair attacks sulfur of SOCl₂, and a Cl leaves as Cl⁻.
why: S is δ+ (bonded to O and two Cl), so it's a good [[electrophile]]. Some books show this as attack at S=O first; the result is the same.

socl2_done.text: The O is bonded to S and carries a + (it has three bonds).
why: The next step is just removing the extra H⁺.

socl2_deprot.text: [[proton transfer|Proton transfer]]: pyridine takes the H⁺. The result is an alkyl chlorosulfite, R–O–S(O)Cl: a good leaving group. Cl⁻ is the nucleophile for step 2.
why: With pyridine the next step is SN2 (inversion). Without pyridine some books describe retention (an SNi mechanism); that case is not covered here.

tscl_attack.text: Step 1 of 2: the O's lone pair attacks sulfur of tosyl chloride (TsCl), and Cl⁻ leaves.
why: The S is δ+ (two S=O and a Cl pull electrons away), so the O lone pair attacks it.

tscl_done.text: The O is bonded to the tosyl group and carries a + (three bonds). Pyridine is there to take the extra H⁺.
why: Pyridine is a weak base that mops up the H⁺ (as pyridinium chloride).

tscl_deprot.text: [[proton transfer|Proton transfer]]: pyridine removes the H⁺. The alcohol is now a [[tosylate]] (R–OTs).
why: This is a fast acid–base step.

tscl_result.text: Product: {product}. The C–O bond was never broken, so the carbon keeps its configuration ([[retention]]). TsO⁻ is an excellent leaving group: now pick a nucleophile for step 2 (that step will invert the carbon).
why: OTs is as good a leaving group as I⁻ (or better), because TsO⁻ is a very weak base (its charge is spread over three O's).

sn1_meet_ion.text: {Nu} arrives. The C⁺ is so electron-poor that it grabs almost any lone pair, so the nucleophile that bumps into it first wins.
why: Because the cation is so reactive, SN1 doesn't need a strong nucleophile: the slow step was the leaving group going.

stereo.inversion: The carbon was {from}; after inversion it is {to}.
stereo.inversion_same: The groups inverted. The letter stays {to} here because the new group changes the priorities.
stereo.inversion_cistrans: The ring carbon inverted, so cis becomes trans (or trans becomes cis).
stereo.undefined: The starting carbon was drawn without wedges, so no stereo is claimed. With wedges you'd see inversion.
stereo.none: The reacting carbon is not a stereocentre, so there's nothing to invert visibly.
stereo.racemic: The flat C⁺ was attacked from both faces, so both configurations at that carbon form (racemic there; with another stereocentre present, a mixture of diastereomers).
stereo.sn1_none: The carbon that was attacked is not a stereocentre in the product, so there's no stereo to report.
stereo.ez_unknown: The E/Z geometry here depends on the 3D arrangement, which isn't covered yet, so no E/Z is claimed.

glossary.nucleophile: Nucleophile (Nu): an electron-rich species that donates an electron pair to form a new bond with an electron-poor atom. 'Nucleus-loving'.
glossary.electrophile: Electrophile: an electron-poor atom or molecule that accepts an electron pair. Here, the δ+ carbon bonded to the leaving group.
glossary.electronegativity: Electronegativity: how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons towards itself. F > O > Cl > N > Br > I > C > H.
glossary.backside attack: Backside attack: the nucleophile approaches the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group (180°). Required for SN2.
glossary.antibonding orbital: Antibonding orbital (σ*): an empty orbital of the C–LG bond. Filling it with the nucleophile's electrons breaks the C–LG bond.
glossary.transition state: Transition state (‡): the highest-energy arrangement along the path, with bonds partly made and partly broken. It lasts for one vibration and can't be isolated.
glossary.bimolecular: Bimolecular: two species (nucleophile and substrate) take part in the slow step, so rate = k[substrate][Nu].
glossary.leaving group: Leaving group (LG): the atom or group that leaves with the bonding electron pair. Good LGs are weak bases: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻, and sulfonates (OTs, OMs). OH⁻ and F⁻ are poor.
glossary.Walden inversion: Walden inversion: the three groups on the attacked carbon flip to the other side, like an umbrella turning inside out. Every SN2 does this.
glossary.stereospecific: Stereospecific: each stereoisomer of the starting material gives a specific stereoisomer of the product (SN2, E2). SN1 is not: it gives both.
glossary.carbocation: Carbocation: a carbon with only three bonds, six electrons and a + charge. Flat (sp²) with an empty p orbital. Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl; allylic/benzylic are extra stable.
glossary.hyperconjugation: Hyperconjugation: neighbouring C–H and C–C bonds share a little of their electron density with an empty p orbital, stabilising a carbocation. More neighbouring carbons → more stabilisation.
glossary.intermediate: Intermediate: a real species in a dip of the energy diagram (e.g. a carbocation). Unlike a transition state, it can live long enough to react in different ways.
glossary.rate-determining step: Rate-determining step: the slowest step (the highest hump). Its reactants set the rate law.
glossary.unimolecular: Unimolecular: only one species takes part in the slow step, so rate = k[substrate]. The 1 in SN1 and E1.
glossary.resonance: Resonance: when one structure can be drawn in two or more ways that differ only in where electrons are. The real species is a blend; spreading charge stabilises it.
glossary.1,2-shift: 1,2-shift: an H (as hydride), alkyl group or ring bond moves with its electron pair from a carbon to the neighbouring C⁺, making a more stable cation.
glossary.ring expansion: Ring expansion: a 1,2-shift of a ring bond to a C⁺ just outside the ring. The ring grows by one carbon (e.g. 5 → 6), relieving ring strain.
glossary.ring strain: Ring strain: extra energy in small rings from squeezed bond angles and eclipsed bonds. Cyclopropane > cyclobutane > cyclopentane > cyclohexane (almost none).
glossary.protic solvent: Polar protic solvent: has O–H or N–H (water, alcohols). Stabilises ions and carbocations, and cages anionic nucleophiles with hydrogen bonds.
glossary.solvolysis: Solvolysis: a reaction where the solvent (water, an alcohol) is the nucleophile.
glossary.racemic: Racemic: a 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers. Optically inactive; drawn with plain lines on worksheets.
glossary.oxonium ion: Oxonium ion: an oxygen with three bonds and a + charge (e.g. R–OH₂⁺).
glossary.proton transfer: Proton transfer: an H⁺ moves from one atom to another (an acid–base step). Fast; many worksheets say to neglect these steps.
glossary.base: Base: a species that removes a proton (H⁺) with its lone pair. Strong bases (HO⁻, RO⁻, t-BuO⁻) favour E2.
glossary.anti-periplanar: Anti-periplanar: the H and the leaving group are in one plane, 180° apart (on opposite sides of the C–C bond). Required for E2.
glossary.Zaitsev's rule: Zaitsev's rule: in elimination the more substituted alkene (more carbons on the C=C) is usually major, because it is more stable.
glossary.Hofmann product: Hofmann product: the less substituted alkene, which becomes major with a bulky base (t-BuO⁻) that takes the most reachable H.
glossary.entropy: Entropy: disorder. Elimination makes more molecules than it uses, so higher temperature (heat) favours it.
glossary.catalyst: Catalyst: speeds up a reaction and is given back at the end (like H⁺ in acid-catalysed dehydration).
glossary.tosylate: Tosylate (OTs): a p-toluenesulfonate ester, R–O–SO₂–C₆H₄–CH₃. An excellent leaving group made from an alcohol and TsCl without touching the C–O bond.
glossary.retention: Retention: the carbon keeps its original 3D arrangement (no bonds to it were broken).

substrate.methyl: Methyl: no carbons on the reacting carbon, so the back is wide open. SN2 only; a methyl cation is far too unstable for SN1.
substrate.1: 1° (primary): one carbon on the reacting carbon. The back is open, so SN2 is fast; a 1° cation is too unstable for SN1 (unless allylic/benzylic).
substrate.2: 2° (secondary): two carbons on the reacting carbon. Every path is possible, so the reagent and solvent decide.
substrate.3: 3° (tertiary): three carbons block the back, so no SN2. The 3° cation is stable, so SN1/E1, or E2 with a strong base.
substrate.vinyl: The leaving group is on a C=C carbon (vinyl). No SN1, SN2, E1 or E2 here.
substrate.aryl: The leaving group is on a benzene ring carbon (aryl). No SN1, SN2, E1 or E2 here.

reagent.nuc: Strong nucleophile, weak base: it prefers to attack carbon (substitution) rather than pull off a proton.
reagent.nucbase: Strong nucleophile and strong base: substitution and elimination compete; the substrate class decides.
reagent.bulky: Strong but bulky base: too crowded to reach carbon, so it pulls off the most reachable β-H (elimination).
reagent.weak: Weak nucleophile, weak base (neutral): it waits for a carbocation to form first (SN1/E1).
reagent.activator: Turns the poor OH leaving group into a good one first.

solvent.protic: Polar protic solvent (has O–H): stabilises ions and the carbocation, and 'cages' the nucleophile with hydrogen bonds. Favours SN1/E1.
solvent.aprotic: Polar aprotic solvent (no O–H): dissolves salts but leaves the anion 'naked' and reactive. Favours SN2/E2.
solvent.heat: Heat favours elimination, because it makes more molecules (entropy).

ui.comingSoon: The {pw} animation for this case isn't available yet. The prediction and products above are already from the rules.
ui.rankingMode: {n} molecules in the editor: ranking mode. Draw one molecule to predict a reaction.
ui.noName: No name: PubChem has no record and the built-in namer can't name it.
ui.offerMajor: {other} is the major path here. See it?

attack.explain: {Nu} attacks the δ+ carbon that holds {LG} (Cα), from the back side.

attack_cation.q: Quiz: which carbon will {Nu} bond to? Tap it.
attack_cation.explain: The nucleophile bonds to the carbon that carries the + (the empty p orbital).

shift.q: Quiz: will this {cation} cation rearrange (shift)? Yes or No.
shift.explainYes: Yes: a neighbouring H, CH₃ or ring bond can move over and give a more stable cation, so it shifts.
shift.explainYesNotTaken: Yes, it can: a shift gives a more stable cation, and that is the major path. This card follows the other path, where {Nu} traps the cation before it shifts (minor product).
shift.explainNo: No: no neighbouring H, CH₃ or ring bond can move to make a more stable cation, so it stays put.

beta_e1.q: Quiz: which carbon loses an H to give the major alkene? Tap it.
beta_e1.explain: The H comes from the β-carbon that gives the more substituted, more stable alkene (Zaitsev).

beta_e2.q: Quiz: which carbon loses an H to give the major alkene? Tap it.
beta_e2.explain: Small strong base: the β-carbon giving the more substituted alkene (Zaitsev). Bulky base: the most reachable β-H, usually on the end CH₃ (Hofmann).

activate_o.q: Quiz: which atom of the alcohol does the reagent react with first? Tap it.
activate_o.explain: The O: its lone pairs attack the reagent. The C–O bond is not touched in this step.

attack_allyl.q: Quiz: which carbon can {Nu} bond to? Tap one.
attack_allyl.explain: Either end: the + is shared by both ends of the allylic cation (resonance), so {Nu} can bond at either one. That is why two products form.

compete._about: Key 'major>minor': why the minor pathway is minor here. Shown after the offer line.
compete.SN1>E1: Same carbocation, different ending: the solvent can pull off a β-H instead of bonding to C⁺. Your course counts substitution as the major answer for a weak nucleophile in a protic solvent; heat makes E1 more important.
compete.E1>SN1: Same carbocation: with heat and a poor nucleophile, losing a β-H wins over being trapped.
compete.SN2>E2: {Nu} is a base as well as a nucleophile, but this {class} carbon's back side is open enough that substitution wins.
compete.E2>SN2: {Nu} can also attack carbon, but the {class} carbon is crowded and/or the base is strong or bulky, so taking a β-H is easier.
compete.generic: Both pathways happen with these conditions; the lamps show which one is major.

reagentTypes._about: Shown when a reagent isn't in the catalogue: how to recognise each of the four types, and what it does. Same four boxes the rules use (docs/mechanisms-plan.md).
reagentTypes.intro: How to tell which type a reagent is:

nuc.name: Strong Nu, weak base
nuc.spot: A negative charge on S, N, C or a halide (I⁻, Br⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻), or a carboxylate (RCOO⁻). The charge is on a big or well-stabilised atom, so it doesn't want an H⁺ much.
nuc.does: Attacks carbon: SN2 at methyl/1°/2°. With 3° it can't reach the back, so it waits for SN1 in a protic solvent.

nucbase.name: Strong Nu + strong base
nucbase.spot: A negative O on H or a small carbon: HO⁻, CH₃O⁻, EtO⁻.
nucbase.does: Can attack carbon or pull off a β-H: SN2 wins at 1°, E2 wins at 2° and 3°.

bulky.name: Bulky strong base
bulky.spot: A negative O on a crowded (tertiary) carbon, like t-BuO⁻, or a hindered neutral base like DBU.
bulky.does: Too crowded to reach carbon, so it pulls off the most reachable β-H: E2, often the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene.

weak.name: Weak Nu / weak base
weak.spot: A neutral molecule with an O–H: water or an alcohol. No charge.
weak.does: Too weak to push anything out. It waits for a carbocation: SN1/E1 at 2° and 3° (or allylic/benzylic) in a protic solvent.
